subject: english
competencies: S: The learners will demonstrate the following:
contentSummary: Overview: Note-taking is writing down important points from a story, lesson or text so you can remember them later. In this lesson, learners will demonstrate note-taking skills after learning shorthand techniques that include abbreviations, shorthand, SMS language and acronyms. They will practice writing notes from oral sources like the teacher, radio, Bluetooth messages or speeches. These skills will help learners record important points quickly and clearly. (Consolidation):  Model taking notes  Emphasise taking important points only, not every word.  Encourage learners to use symbols and letters for faster writing. Tip: Before reading the story aloud, ask the learners to listen attentively and take notes of the important points using shorthand techniques.  Teacher to read the story below aloud Mukwena’s Fruit Stand Mukwena wanted to earn some money. He decided to sell bananas and oranges in front of his house. Every morning, Mukwena picked fresh fruits from his garden. He washed them and put them in baskets. Each basket was tagged with a price: bananas, 5 kwacha; oranges, 10 kwacha. People walking by stopped to buy his fruits. Mukwena greeted every customer politely. For each sale, he kept track of how many fruits he sold and how much money he earned. At the end of the week, Mukwena counted his money. He was very happy because he earned enough to buy books and pencils for school. (Consolidation):  Emphasise listening carefully to pick out important points.  Show learners how to use shorthand: symbols, abbreviations or short forms.  Encourage using keywords only, not full sentences.
learnerActivities: a: Discussing shorthand skills for note-taking (abbreviations, short forms,
assessmentCriteria: Notes from oral sources written correctly
exercises: i. Did they write key points only?
ii. Did they use shorthand correctly?
iii. Are the notes organised and understandable?
iv. Ask learners to read their notes aloud and explain their story briefly.

contentSummary: Overview Page 43 of 82 Action verbs are words that describe a physical or mental action performed by the subject of the sentence. An action verb is the engine of a sentence. Every complete sentence has parts, the subject (who or what the sentence is about) and the predicate (what the subject does or is). In this topic, learners will discover that an action verb describes what the subject of a sentence performs, expressing physical or mental actions. (Consolidation):  Explain that an action verb must show that someone or something is doing something.  Use action and movements to emphasise on action verbs.  Use simple and familiar words that are applicable in real-life situations. contentSummary: OVERVIEW Linking verbs are verbs that connect the subject of a sentence to a word or phrase that describes or identifies the subject. Unlike action verbs, they do not show action but instead serve as a bridge between the subject and additional information about it. Understanding linking verbs is important because they help learners form clear, descriptive sentences and improve their writing by showing relationships between subjects and their qualities or states. Linking verbs also help us communicate clearly. (consolidation)  Explain that linking verbs connect the subject to a word that describes or identifies it..  Give learners sentences with linking verbs and action verbs. Ask them to sort the verbs into two groups. Remind them that linking verbs tell what the subject is, while action verbs tell what the subject does.
